claims.claim: TRP channels are a large and diverse family of cation permeable ion channel proteins that are expressed in animals and yeast, algae and other unicellular organisms.
claims.source: Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels are a large and diverse family of cation permeable ion channel proteins that are expressed in animals and yeast, algae and other unicellular organisms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement from the introduction that cites established knowledge about TRP channel expression patterns.

claims.claim: The biological functions of TRP channels include nociception, thermosensation, immune cell function, control of cellular excitability, fluid secretion, cardiac and smooth muscle function and development, ion homeostasis and lysosomal function.
claims.source: The biological functions of TRP channels are remarkably diverse, and include nociception, thermosensation, immune cell function, control of cellular excitability, fluid secretion, cardiac and smooth muscle function and development, ion homeostasis and lysosomal function (Nilius and Flockerzi, 2014; Ramsey et al., 2006; Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The TRP family name is derived from the Drosophila mutant that causes blindness in which neurons exhibit a transient receptor potential instead of a persistent response to illumination.
claims.source: The family name is derived from the Drosophila mutant that causes blindness in which the neurons of mutant flies exhibit a transient receptor potential (trp) instead of a persistent response to illumination with intense light in electroretinograms (Cosens and Manning, 1969).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by a citation.

claims.claim: TRP channels have been classified into seven subfamilies: TRPC (canonical), TRPV (vanilloid), TRPM (melastatin), TRPA (ankyrin), TRPN (NOMPC), TRPP (polycystic) and TRPML (mucolipin).
claims.source: TRP channels have been classified into seven subfamilies: TRPC (canonical), TRPV (vanilloid), TRPM (melastatin), TRPA (ankyrin), TRPN (NOMPC), TRPP (polycystic) and TRPML (mucolipin) (Clapham, 2007).
claims.evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Mutations in TRP channels cause a range of human diseases and are considered important drug targets for pain, inflammation, asthma, cancer, anxiety, cardiac disease and metabolic disorders.
claims.source: As expected from their widespread expression and physiological roles, mutations in TRP channels cause a range of human diseases and are considered important drug targets for pain, inflammation, asthma, cancer, anxiety, cardiac disease and metabolic disorders (Moran, 2018; Nilius et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The structure of TRPV1 determined in 2013 ushered in a new era for solving near-atomic resolution structures of membrane proteins using cryo-electron microscopy.
claims.source: TRP channels have a notable historical significance in membrane protein structural biology because the structure of TRPV1 determined in 2013 ushered in a new era for solving near-atomic resolution structures of membrane proteins using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original TRPV1 structure papers.

claims.claim: At least one structure has been reported for each TRP channel subfamily, with a total of 136 TRP channel structures available at the time of analysis.
claims.source: At least one structure has now been reported for each subfamily, with a total of 136 TRP channel structures available at the time we performed this analysis (Autzen et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2017; Dang et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2018; Diver et al., 2019; Dosey et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2018b; Duan et al., 2018c; Fan et al., 2018; Grieben et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; Hirschi et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2018a; Hughes et al., 2018b; Hulse et al., 2018; Huynh et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2013; McGoldrick et al., 2019; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Paulsen et al., 2015; Saotome et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018a; Singh et al., 2018b; Singh et al., 2018c; Su et al., 2018a; Su et al., 2018b; Tang et al., 2018; Vinayagam et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Wilkes et al., 2017; Winkler et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2019b; Yin et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2017; Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018a; Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: TRP channels are tetramers, with each subunit containing six transmembrane helices (S1-S6).
claims.source: These structures show that TRP channels are tetramers, with each subunit containing six transmembrane (TM) helices (S1-S6), and with the S5 and S6 helices from the four subunits forming a central pore domain containing the ion permeation pathway (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to structural data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The S5 and S6 helices from the four subunits form a central pore domain containing the ion permeation pathway.
claims.source: These structures show that TRP channels are tetramers, with each subunit containing six transmembrane (TM) helices (S1-S6), and with the S5 and S6 helices from the four subunits forming a central pore domain containing the ion permeation pathway (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to structural data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The S1-S4 helices form peripheral domains within the membrane with a domain-swapped architecture such that each S1-S4 domain is positioned near to the pore-forming S5-S6 helices from the adjacent subunit.
claims.source: The S1-S4 helices form peripheral domains within the membrane with a domain-swapped architecture such that each S1-S4 domain is positioned near to the pore-forming S5-S6 helices from the adjacent subunit (Figure 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to structural data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claims.claim: Most TRP channels contain a highly conserved helical extension of the pore-lining S6 helix named the TRP box that projects through a tunnel formed by the intracellular-facing surface of the S1-S4 domain and the pre-S1 region of the N-terminus.
claims.source: Most TRP channels also contain a highly conserved helical extension of the pore-lining S6 helix named the TRP box that projects through a tunnel formed by the intracellular-facing surface of the S1-S4 domain and the pre-S1 region of the N-terminus (Figure 1F,I–M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to structural data shown in Figure 1F,I–M.

claims.claim: A structure-based alignment of the transmembrane domains of 120 TRP channel structures was constructed.
claims.source: To facilitate mechanistic investigations, we constructed a structure-based alignment of the transmembrane domains of 120 TRP channel structures.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological claim describing what the authors did in this study.

claims.claim: Comparison of structures determined in the absence or presence of activating stimuli reveals similar constrictions in the central ion permeation pathway near the intracellular end of the S6 helices.
claims.source: Comparison of structures determined in the absence or presence of activating stimuli reveals similar constrictions in the central ion permeation pathway near the intracellular end of the S6 helices, pointing to a conserved cytoplasmic gate and suggesting that most available structures represent non-conducting states.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of structural data.

claims.claim: Most available TRP channel structures represent non-conducting states.
claims.source: Comparison of structures determined in the absence or presence of activating stimuli reveals similar constrictions in the central ion permeation pathway near the intracellular end of the S6 helices, pointing to a conserved cytoplasmic gate and suggesting that most available structures represent non-conducting states.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis of pore dimensions.

claims.claim: Sequence-based alignment of TRP channels is complicated by low sequence identity, with a previous multiple sequence alignment revealing just 16% identity as the major mode.
claims.source: Sequence-based alignment of TRP channels is complicated by low sequence identity, with a previous multiple sequence alignment of TRP channel TM sequences revealing just 16% identity as the major mode of the full multiple sequence alignment (Palovcak et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Structure-based alignments are thought to be more reliable than sequence-based alignments, particularly when sequence identity is low.
claims.source: Structure-based alignments are thought to be more reliable than sequence-based alignments, particularly when sequence identity is low (Carpentier and Chomilier, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: A total of 136 TRP channel structures had been reported at the time of this analysis, of which 117 were determined using cryo-EM and 22 using X-ray diffraction.
claims.source: A total of 136 TRP channel structures had been reported at the time of this analysis, of which 117 were determined using cryo-EM and 22 using X-ray diffraction.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset used in the study.

claims.claim: 120 TRP channel structures resolved to effective resolutions of 5 Å or better were selected for analysis.
claims.source: We therefore selected 120 of those structures that were resolved to effective resolutions of 5 Å or better (Figure 2—source data 1) and focused on the TM region, which appears to have a well-conserved architecture across TRP channels.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the selection criteria for structures.

claims.claim: The TM regions of TRP channels were aligned using Fr-TM-Align, which aligns structures pairwise by optimizing for the global template-modeling-score (TM-score).
claims.source: The TM regions of these channels were aligned using Fr-TM-Align (Pandit and Skolnick, 2008; Zhang and Skolnick, 2005), which aligns structures pairwise by optimizing for the global template-modeling-score (TM-score), a measure of backbone fold similarity that is independent of protein length (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement with citations to the alignment method.

claims.claim: Alignments of the TM regions of the TRP family structures generally have TM-scores of >0.6, indicating that they share similar global folds.
claims.source: Alignments of the TM regions of the TRP family structures generally have TM-scores of >0.6, indicating that they share similar global folds (Figure 2; Xu and Zhang, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the TM-score analysis shown in Figure 2 and cited interpretation criteria.

claims.claim: The aligned TRP channel structures share a common fold with a voltage-activated potassium channel (2r9r), with TM-scores ranging from 0.46 to 0.78.
claims.source: The aligned TRP channel structures also share a common fold with a voltage-activated potassium channel (2r9r; TM-scores ranging from 0.46 to 0.78, with TM-scores <0.6 obtained only for some TRPM and TRPC structures), consistent with them sharing six TM helices per subunit, a common tetrameric assembly and a domain-swapped architecture.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on TM-score analysis comparing TRP channels to a Kv channel.

claims.claim: Clustering based on TM-score corresponded to existing subfamily assignments for TRP channels.
claims.source: With a few notable exceptions, clustering based on TM-score corresponded nicely to existing subfamily assignments, despite the variety of methods of structure determination (X-ray vs cryo-EM) and imaging environments (detergent, amphipol, or nanodisc) used, suggesting that the conditions of structure determination have not introduced substantial artifacts (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The pore domains in TRP channels are highly conserved across all TRP channel subfamilies on the sequence level.
claims.source: On the sequence level, the pore domains in TRP channels are highly conserved across all TRP channel subfamilies, whereas the peripheral S1-S4 domains are more variable between subfamilies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; sequence identity data from Fr-TM-Align pairwise alignments not shown) (Ng et al., 2019; Palovcak et al., 2015; Vinayagam et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The peripheral S1-S4 domains are more variable between subfamilies than the pore domains.
claims.source: On the sequence level, the pore domains in TRP channels are highly conserved across all TRP channel subfamilies, whereas the peripheral S1-S4 domains are more variable between subfamilies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; sequence identity data from Fr-TM-Align pairwise alignments not shown) (Ng et al., 2019; Palovcak et al., 2015; Vinayagam et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Clustering of TRP channel structures into subfamilies was more robust when considering the TM-scores of the peripheral S1-S4 domains compared to those of the pore domain.
claims.source: Consistent with this pattern, clustering of TRP channel structures into subfamilies was more robust when considering the TM-scores of the peripheral S1-S4 domains compared to those of the pore domain (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claims.claim: The structure of Xenopus laevis TRPV4 (6bbj) is a notable exception in hierarchical clustering, with unusually low TM-scores when aligned with other TRPV channels.
claims.source: In the hierarchical clustering of the entire TM region, the structures determined for Xenopus laevis TRPV4 (6bbj) and the rTRPV6 L495Q mutant (5iwk) are notable exceptions because the TM-scores of their alignments with the other TRPV channels were unusually low (0.41 to 0.77 for TRPV4 and 0.32 to 0.73 for rTRPV6 L495Q) (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on TM-score analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The rTRPV6 L495Q mutant adopts a non-domain-swapped architecture unlike the wild-type protein.
claims.source: When the pore domain and S1-S4 domains were considered separately, the rTRPV6 L495Q mutant did cluster with the vanilloid subfamily (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), consistent with the individual domains adopting similar folds and with the global fold dissimilarity in the whole TM region stemming from the rTRPV6 L495Q mutant adopting a non-domain-swapped architecture unlike the wild-type protein (Saotome et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Functional studies have concluded that the TRPV1 channel opens and closes at the intracellular end of the pore in response to vanilloid binding.
claims.source: With respect to the latter, functional studies examining the accessibility of introduced cysteine residues to thiol-reactive compounds and metals (Salazar et al., 2009), as well as studies examining the state-dependence of blocking ions (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2008; Oseguera et al., 2007), have concluded that the TRPV1 channel opens and closes at the intracellular end of the pore in response to vanilloid binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: A similar S6 activation gate region has been identified in structures determined in the absence of activating ligands for all TRP channel subfamilies, with the exception of a few that have high baseline activity, such as TRPV5 and TRPV6.
claims.source: A similar S6 activation gate region has been identified in studies of structures determined in the absence of activating ligands for all TRP channel subfamilies, with the exception of a few that have high baseline activity, such as TRPV5 and TRPV6 (Chen et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; Hirschi et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2017; Liao et al., 2013; Paulsen et al., 2015; Schmiege et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2018; Winkler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claims.claim: In all TRP channel structures analyzed, the intracellular S6 constrictions occur at one or more of four positions spanning three helical turns of the S6 helix.
claims.source: In all structures, the intracellular S6 constrictions occur at one or more of four positions spanning three helical turns of the S6 helix, suggesting that depending on the S6 helix conformation, a cytosolic gate could be formed at different sites (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on pore radius analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: 38 out of 55 apo state TRP channel structures contain multiple regions along the intracellular side of the S6 helix at which the pore radius is ≤1.0 Å, too narrow to support permeation of hydrated cations.
claims.source: If we consider only the 55 TRP channel structures with no ligands modeled in the structure as representing apo states (see Materials and methods, Figure 2—source data 1), 38 contain multiple regions along the intracellular side of the S6 helix at which the pore radius is ≤1.0 Å, too narrow to support permeation of hydrated cations (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 4), even considering the inherent dynamics of the structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on pore radius analysis of apo structures.

claims.claim: Most TRP channel structures likely represent non-conducting states where the S6 gate is closed.
claims.source: Given that the internal pores in all TRP channels are lined by hydrophobic residues (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and thus would not attract ions nor facilitate ion dehydration, it seems likely that most of the TRP channel structures discussed thus far represent non-conducting states where the S6 gate is closed.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on pore dimensions and hydrophobicity analysis.

claims.claim: TRPV6 has a relatively high open probability in cellular membranes (0.25–0.9 depending on voltage and the concentration of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate).
claims.source: TRPV6 is interesting because this channel has a relatively high open probability in cellular membranes (0.25–0.9 depending on voltage and the concentration of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, abbreviated PIP2) (Zakharian et al., 2011), and therefore one would expect the structures would be more likely to correspond to open conformations than for other TRP channels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: Two structures of wild-type human TRPV6 and one of the Y467A mutant contain S6 gates with minimal radii of 2.7–3.1 Å, suggesting that they may represent an open, ion-conducting state.
claims.source: However, in all these cases, the protein used for structure determination contained truncations or mutations that might have influenced the closed-open equilibrium. In contrast, two structures of wild-type human TRPV6 and one of the Y467A mutant contain S6 gates with minimal radii of 2.7–3.1 Å, suggesting that they may represent an open, ion-conducting state (McGoldrick et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on pore radius measurements and citation to structural data.

claims.claim: 16 out of 35 activator-bound TRP channel structures contain pores narrower than 1.0 Å radius in the cytoplasmic region, suggesting that they represent non-conducting (possibly desensitized) states.
claims.source: When considering those structures determined in the presence of activators (Figure 2—source data 1), it is notable that 16 out of 35 contain pores narrower than 1.0 Å radius in the cytoplasmic region, suggesting that they represent non-conducting (possibly desensitized) states (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 2, 3; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on pore radius analysis of activator-bound structures.

claims.claim: The structure of zebrafish TRPM2 bound to its two activators (ADP-ribose and Ca2+, 6drj) is the most likely to represent an open state among all TRP channel structures reported.
claims.source: Of all the TRP channel structures reported thus far, that of zebrafish TRPM2 bound to its two activators (ADP-ribose and Ca2+, 6drj) is the most likely to represent an open state, as the dimensions of the S6 gate region of zebrafish TRPM2 (4.4 Å radius) (Huang et al., 2018) are similar to those of Kv channel structures widely considered to be open (4.2–15 Å radius) (Hite and MacKinnon, 2017; Long et al., 2007; Tao et al., 2017; Tao and MacKinnon, 2019b; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of pore dimensions with Kv channels.

claims.claim: The single channel conductance of TRPV1 is quite high (90–100 pS at positive voltages).
claims.source: In the case of TRPV1, not only is the single channel conductance quite high (90–100 pS at positive voltages) (Hui et al., 2003; Oseguera et al., 2007; Premkumar et al., 2002), but also quaternary ammonium blocking ions as large as tetrapentyl ammonium (10 Å diameter) must be able to pass the S6 gate when open (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2008; Oseguera et al., 2007), suggesting that the cytoplasmic pore is likely to be larger than a minimal radius of 3 Å.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: Quaternary ammonium blocking ions as large as tetrapentyl ammonium (10 Å diameter) must be able to pass the S6 gate of TRPV1 when open.
claims.source: In the case of TRPV1, not only is the single channel conductance quite high (90–100 pS at positive voltages) (Hui et al., 2003; Oseguera et al., 2007; Premkumar et al., 2002), but also quaternary ammonium blocking ions as large as tetrapentyl ammonium (10 Å diameter) must be able to pass the S6 gate when open (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2008; Oseguera et al., 2007), suggesting that the cytoplasmic pore is likely to be larger than a minimal radius of 3 Å.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: There was no striking correlation between the dimensions of the internal pore and whether the protein structure was determined in the absence or presence of activators or inhibitors.
claims.source: Surprisingly, there was no striking correlation between the dimensions of the internal pore and whether the protein structure was determined in the absence or presence of activators or inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The prevalence of a cytoplasmic constriction across TRP channel subfamilies supports the prevailing idea that the internal region of S6 functions as a universal gate.
claims.source: The prevalence of a cytoplasmic constriction across TRP channel subfamilies supports the prevailing idea that the internal region of S6 functions as a universal gate, and it seems likely that in most instances the structure of a fully open state remains to be determined.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis and comparison to existing hypotheses.

claims.claim: The extracellular end of the ion permeation pathway is relatively narrow in most structures and across TRP channel subfamilies, consistent with this region serving as an ion selectivity filter.
claims.source: The extracellular end of the ion permeation pathway is relatively narrow in most structures and across TRP channel subfamilies (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), consistent with this region serving as an ion selectivity filter as it does in related tetrameric cation channels (Owsianik et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and citation to prior knowledge.

claims.claim: The ion selectivity of TRP channels fits into three broad categories: Ca2+ selective (TRPV5 and TRPV6), monovalent cation selective (TRPM4 and TRPM5), and non-selective among cations (all other TRP channels).
claims.source: The ion selectivity of TRP channels fits into three broad categories: Ca2+ selective (TRPV5 and TRPV6), monovalent cation selective (TRPM4 and TRPM5), and non-selective among cations (all other TRP channels) (Owsianik et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Non-selective TRP channels have a highly conserved Gly residue after the C-terminal end of the reentrant pore helix that enables a sharp bend in the backbone.
claims.source: First, a highly conserved Gly residue (G643 in TRPV1) is present in non-selective channels after the C-terminal end of the reentrant pore helix that enables a sharp bend in the backbone of the protein (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Non-selective TRP channels have two backbone carbonyls positioned towards the base of the filter where they could interact with permeant ions.
claims.source: Second, two backbone carbonyls are positioned towards the base of the filter where they could interact with permeant ions (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Non-selective TRP channels have the side chain of an acidic residue or a Gln positioned immediately adjacent to the extracellular side of the narrowest region of the filter.
claims.source: Third, the side chain of an acidic residue or a Gln is positioned immediately adjacent to the extracellular side of the narrowest region of the filter (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Mutagenesis of the conserved Asp in TRPV1 and TRPV4 channels reduces divalent ion permeability and channel affinity for the inhibitor ruthenium red.
claims.source: Mutagenesis of the conserved Asp in TRPV1 and TRPV4 channels reduces divalent ion permeability and channel affinity for the inhibitor ruthenium red (García-Martínez et al., 2000; Voets et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: All three structural features seen in non-selective TRP channels are discernably different in the two Ca2+-selective channels, TRPV5 and TRPV6.
claims.source: Notably, all three of these structural features seen in non-selective TRP channels are discernably different in the two Ca2+-selective channels, TRPV5 and TRPV6, as originally noted for the X-ray structure of TRPV6 (Saotome et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural comparison and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: TRPV5 and TRPV6 contain a conserved Thr residue in place of the conserved Gly after the reentrant pore helix, which contributes its hydroxyl group to the ion permeation pathway.
claims.source: In place of the conserved Gly after the reentrant pore helix, TRPV5 and TRPV6 contain a conserved Thr residue that contributes its hydroxyl group to the ion permeation pathway (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Ca2+-selective TRPV5 and TRPV6 channels have a more extended selectivity filter that contains at least three backbone carbonyl groups positioned to line the permeation pathway.
claims.source: In addition, these Ca2+-selective channels have a more extended selectivity filter that contains at least three backbone carbonyl groups positioned to line the permeation pathway (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Mutagenesis of the conserved Asp in the selectivity filter diminishes Ca2+ permeation and Mg2+ block in TRPV5.
claims.source: The conserved Asp or Gln residues found in the non-selective cation permeable TRP channels is always an Asp in TRPV5 and TRPV6, and mutagenesis of this Asp is known to diminish Ca2+ permeation and Mg2+ block in TRPV5 (Nilius et al., 2001)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: Density attributable to a divalent ion was identified in the external narrow region of the selectivity filter in the X-ray structure of rat TRPV6.
claims.source: Finally, the pore radius is consistently narrower at this region of the filter for those two Ca2+ selective channels (Figure 4; Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1); indeed, density attributable to a divalent ion was identified in this external narrow region in the X-ray structure of rat TRPV6 (Saotome et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on structural data and citation to the TRPV6 structure.

claims.claim: The structures of monovalent cation-selective TRPM4 channel exhibit most of the key features seen in the structures of non-selective TRP channels.
claims.source: The structures of the monovalent cation-selective TRPM4 channel from human and mouse are intriguing because these channels exhibit most of the key features seen in the structures of non-selective TRP channels, including the conserved first Gly and two backbone carbonyls within the permeation pathway, and the conserved acidic/Gln position at the external end of the filter is always a Gln (Figure 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The side chain of the conserved Gln in TRPM4 hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl of the conserved first Gly in adjacent subunits, stabilizing the filter with a diameter large enough to support permeation of hydrated monovalent ions.
claims.source: The side chain of this Gln was noted to hydrogen bond with the backbone carbonyl of the conserved first Gly in adjacent subunits in one TRPM4 structure, and this network was proposed to stabilize the filter with a diameter large enough to support permeation of hydrated monovalent ions, but not large enough for hydrated divalent ions nor narrow enough to permit ion coordination and dehydration (Autzen et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2018c; Guo et al., 2017; Winkler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in cited structural studies.

claims.claim: Mutation of the conserved Gln to Glu, Asp or Asn disrupts the monovalent cation selectivity of the TRPM4 channel.
claims.source: Mutation of the conserved Gln to Glu, Asp or Asn disrupts the monovalent cation selectivity of the TRPM4 channel (Guo et al., 2017; Nilius et al., 2005), indicating a critical role of this residue and supporting the proposed mechanism of monovalent cation selectivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: In several TRP channel structures, the ion selectivity filters clearly adopt distinct conformations in apo state structures compared to those that have activators bound.
claims.source: In addition to the heterogeneity in dimensions of the selectivity filters noted above, in several TRP channel structures, the ion selectivity filters clearly adopt distinct conformations in apo state structures compared to those that have activators bound.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: In TRPV1, the selectivity filter has a minimum radius of ~0.5 Å in the apo structure but expands to a minimum radius of 2.5 Å in the presence of the activating toxins DkTx and RTx.
claims.source: For example, in the case of TRPV1, the filter has a minimum radius of ~0.5 Å in the apo structure but expands to a minimum radius of 2.5 Å in the presence of the activating toxins double-knot toxin and resiniferatoxin (DkTx and RTx, respectively; Figure 3), leading to the proposal that the selectivity filter in TRPV1 might also serve as a gate that regulates ion permeation (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citation to prior proposals.

claims.claim: Recent functional experiments examining the possible role of the selectivity filter as a gate in TRPV1-3 channels revealed that thiol-reactive Ag+ ions permeated the selectivity filters in the absence of activators.
claims.source: Recent functional experiments examining the possible role of the selectivity filter as a gate in TRPV1-3 channels revealed that thiol-reactive Ag+ ions permeated the selectivity filters in the absence of activators, suggesting that the filters of these channels allow ion permeation in the closed state (Jara-Oseguera et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: 30 out of 120 TRP channel structures were determined in complex with activating ligands contacting the TM region.
claims.source: Out of the 120 available TRP channel structures that we analyzed, 30 were determined in complex with activating ligands contacting the TM region, including vanilloids (e.g. RTx; TRPV1 and TRPV2), DkTx (TRPV1), cooling agents (icilin and WS-12; TRPM8), Ca2+ ions (TRPM2, TRPM4 and TRPM8), cannabidiol (CBD; TRPV2), ML-SA1 (TRPML1), 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB; TRPV3 and TRPV6) and PIP2 (TRPM8) (Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset analyzed.

claims.claim: The vanilloid-binding pocket in TRPV1 is positioned at the interface between the S1-S4 domain of each subunit and the pore-forming S5-S6 domain of the adjacent subunit.
claims.source: The vanilloid-binding pocket observed in the rat TRPV1-RTx complex in nanodiscs (Gao et al., 2016b), and in an engineered rabbit TRPV2 channel in detergent (Zubcevic et al., 2018b), is positioned at the interface between the S1-S4 domain of each subunit and the pore-forming S5-S6 domain of the adjacent subunit, with residues in S3, S4, S4-S5 linker, S5 and S6 contacting RTx (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: RTx contacts the side chains of 15 aliphatic and aromatic hydrophobic residues and four polar or charged residues in the complex with TRPV1.
claims.source: RTx is a relatively large ligand, with a surface area of 1,605 Å2, and it contacts the side chains of 15 aliphatic and aromatic hydrophobic residues and four polar or charged residues in the complex with TRPV1 (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Lipid-facing cavities lined by hydrophobic residues resembling the vanilloid-binding pocket in TRPV1 and TRPV2 can be seen in all TRP channel subfamilies.
claims.source: Notably, lipid-facing cavities lined by hydrophobic residues resembling this vanilloid-binding pocket in TRPV1 and TRPV2 can be seen in all TRP channel subfamilies (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The vanilloids capsaicin and capsazepine have been reported to inhibit TRPM8 channels.
claims.source: Indeed, the vanilloids capsaicin and capsazepine have been reported to inhibit TRPM8 channels (Behrendt et al., 2004; Weil et al., 2005), possibly by binding to the equivalent pocket, although their site and mechanism of action in the TRPM8 channel have yet to be explored.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: DkTx contains two domains, K1 and K2, which bind to the outer perimeter of the pore domain of TRPV1, interacting with residues in the extracellular end of S6 and the reentrant pore helix.
claims.source: DkTx contains two domains, K1 and K2, which bind to the outer perimeter of the pore domain of TRPV1, interacting with residues in the extracellular end of S6 and the reentrant pore helix, as well as with lipids in the surrounding membrane (Figure 7; Bae et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: DkTx is thought to be selective for TRPV1 as the toxin does not activate TRPV2, TRPV3, TRPV4, TRPA1 or TRPM8.
claims.source: DkTx is thought to be selective for TRPV1 as the toxin does not activate TRPV2, TRPV3, TRPV4, TRPA1 or TRPM8 (Bohlen et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: The cooling-agent-binding pocket in TRPM8 is located close to the vanilloid-binding pocket seen in TRPV1 and TRPV2.
claims.source: Cryo-EM structures of flycatcher TRPM8, in complex either with WS-12, a potent analog of menthol, or with both the cooling agent icilin and Ca2+ ions, reveal that the cooling agent binding pocket is located close to the vanilloid-binding pocket seen in TRPV1 and TRPV2 (Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: The cooling-agent-binding pocket in TRPM8 is located entirely within the S1-S4 domain, with residues in all four helices and the TRP box contributing to the site.
claims.source: In contrast to the vanilloid site, however, the cooling-agent-binding pocket is located entirely within the S1-S4 domain, with residues in all four helices and the TRP box contributing to the site (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Residues lining the cooling-agent-binding pocket in TRPM8 are highly conserved in TRPM2 and TRPM4 structures and somewhat conserved in TRPM7 channels.
claims.source: Beyond TRPM8, our analysis shows that residues lining the cooling-agent-binding pocket in TRPM8 are highly conserved in TRPM2 and TRPM4 structures and somewhat conserved in TRPM7 channels, but are very different in TRPV, TRPML and TRPP channels (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Intracellular Ca2+ regulates the activity of TRPM2, TRPM4 and TRPM8 channels.
claims.source: Intracellular Ca2+ regulates the activity of TRPM2, TRPM4 and TRPM8 channels and densities attributed to Ca2+ ions have been identified within the S1-S4 domains of all three TRPM channels (Autzen et al., 2018; Diver et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2019a; Yin et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ binding site in TRPM8 is contiguous with the cooling-agent-binding pocket, though none of the Ca2+-binding residues directly contact the cooling agents WS-12 or icilin.
claims.source: The Ca2+ binding sites identified in these TRPM channels involve Glu, Asp, Gln and Asn residues in S2 and S3, and, in the context of TRPM8, the Ca2+ binding site is contiguous with the cooling-agent-binding pocket, though none of the Ca2+-binding residues directly contact the cooling agents WS-12 or icilin (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The 2-APB-binding sites identified in TRPV3 and TRPV6 channels are located at three distinct sites, designated sites 1–3.
claims.source: The 2-APB-binding sites identified in cryo-EM structures of mouse and human TRPV3 and rat and human TRPV6 channels are noteworthy because this ligand functions as either an activator or inhibitor for many different TRP channels and was observed at three distinct sites, designated sites 1–3 (Figure 9; Singh et al., 2018a; Singh et al., 2018c; Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: Site one for 2-APB in TRPV3 is located within the cytoplasm at the interface between the TRP helix and the pre-S1 helix.
claims.source: Site one in mouse and human TRPV3 is located within the cytoplasm at the interface between the TRP helix and the pre-S1 helix (Figure 9C) and mutations in this site also alter the apparent affinity for 2-APB (Hu et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2018a; Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: Site two for 2-APB in TRPV3 is located near the intracellular end of the TM domains between the S1-S4 domain and the TRP helix.
claims.source: Site two in mouse TRPV3 is located near the intracellular end of the TM domains between the S1-S4 domain and the TRP helix (Figure 9D), in the vicinity of the cooling-agent-binding sites in TRPM8 (Singh et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citation.

claims.claim: Mutation of a conserved Tyr to Ala in site two increases the apparent affinity of 2-APB to TRPV1-3 and to TRPV6, even though the ligand is an activator in TRPV1-3 and an inhibitor in TRPV6.
claims.source: Mutation of a conserved Tyr to Ala in site two increases the apparent affinity of 2-APB to TRPV1-3 and to TRPV6, even though the ligand is an activator in TRPV1-3 and an inhibitor in TRPV6 (Singh et al., 2018c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: Site three for 2-APB in TRPV3 is located toward the extracellular side of the protein between S1 and S3 helices.
claims.source: Site three in mouse TRPV3 is located toward the extracellular side of the protein between S1 and S3 helices, and point mutations in this site decrease 2-APB affinity (Singh et al., 2018a; Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citation to functional studies.

claims.claim: All three 2-APB binding sites in TRPV3 are poorly conserved in other TRP channels when compared to TRPV3.
claims.source: Using our structural alignments, we examined the conservation of all three sites, and found that all three are poorly conserved in other TRP channels (including TRPV6) when compared to TRPV3, and that the 2-APB site in TRPV6 only shows conservation with TRPV5 (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: 2-APB can modulate the activity of many different TRP channels as an agonist or inhibitor depending on the channel.
claims.source: This lack of conservation is surprising given that 2-APB can modulate the activity of many different TRP channels (as an agonist for TRPV1-3 and TRPM6; as an inhibitor of TRPM2, TRPM3, TRPM8, TRPC5, TRPC6 and TRPV6; as an inhibitor at low concentration and as agonist at high concentration for TRPM7) (Chokshi et al., 2012; Colton and Zhu, 2007; Hu et al., 2004; Kovacs et al., 2012; Togashi et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: The phyto-cannabinoid cannabidiol (CBD) was identified in a pocket at the interface between the S6 helix from one subunit and the neighboring pore loop, S5, and S6 helices in structures of rat TRPV2.
claims.source: The phyto-cannabinoid cannabidiol (CBD) was identified in this pocket in structures of rat TRPV2 (Pumroy et al., 2019), and the agonist ML-SA1 was found in the corresponding location in human TRPML1 (Fine et al., 2018; Schmiege et al., 2017; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: The agonist ML-SA1 was found in a pocket at the interface between the S6 helix from one subunit and the neighboring pore loop, S5, and S6 helices in human TRPML1.
claims.source: The phyto-cannabinoid cannabidiol (CBD) was identified in this pocket in structures of rat TRPV2 (Pumroy et al., 2019), and the agonist ML-SA1 was found in the corresponding location in human TRPML1 (Fine et al., 2018; Schmiege et al., 2017; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citations.

claims.claim: A high frequency of π-helix-like elements within a relatively narrow region of S6 is readily apparent across TRP channel structures.
claims.source: A high frequency of π-helix-like elements within a relatively narrow region of S6 is readily apparent, consistent with conclusions from a recent review on the role of this alternative helix conformation in opening of TRP channels (Zubcevic and Lee, 2019c).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on secondary structure analysis and citation to a review.

claims.claim: There is a slight positive correlation between pore radius and the length of the S6 π helices when taking all TRP channel structures together.
claims.source: Taking all structures together, there is a slight positive correlation between pore radius and the length of the S6 π helices (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 310 helices are commonly found at the intracellular end of the S4 helices across all TRP channel subfamilies.
claims.source: We also found that 310 helices are commonly found at the intracellular end of the S4 helices across all TRP channel subfamilies (Figure 10), similar to what has been observed with the corresponding TM helices in voltage-activated ion channels.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on secondary structure analysis shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: 310 helices within S4 are observed regardless of whether structures were determined in the presence or absence of activators.
claims.source: Notably, these 310 helices within S4 are observed regardless of whether structures were determined in the presence or absence of activators (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on secondary structure analysis shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The analysis strongly supports the prevailing view that the intracellular end of the S6 helices forms a constriction or gate that prevents ion permeation in closed or non-conducting desensitized states.
claims.source: Our analysis strongly supports the prevailing view that the intracellular end of the S6 helices forms a constriction or gate that prevents ion permeation in closed or non-conducting desensitized states, with the narrowest constrictions occurring at one of four positions along the S6 helices.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural analysis performed in this study.

claims.claim: The open states for most TRP channels remain to be elucidated based on global analysis of the dimensions of the S6 gate region.
claims.source: In addition, global analysis of the dimensions of the S6 gate region lead us to suggest that the open states for most TRP channels remain to be elucidated.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural analysis performed in this study.

claims.claim: The internal pore of zebrafish TRPM2 when bound by Ca2+ and ADP ribose (6drj) has a radius of 4.4 Å and is likely large enough to permit rapid diffusion of hydrated cations.
claims.source: The internal pore of zebrafish TRPM2 when bound by Ca2+ and ADP ribose (6drj) has a radius of 4.4 Å and thus is likely large enough to permit rapid diffusion of hydrated cations, consistent with this structure representing an open state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on pore radius measurements.

claims.claim: The X-ray structure of rat TRPV6 and a cryo-EM structure of mouse TRPM4 have led to interesting working hypotheses for mechanisms of divalent and monovalent ion selectivity.
claims.source: The X-ray structure of rat TRPV6 (divalent selective) (Saotome et al., 2016) and a cryo-EM structure of mouse TRPM4 (monovalent selective) (Guo et al., 2017 have led to interesting working hypotheses for these two classes of ion selectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about hypotheses derived from cited structural studies.

claims.claim: In TRPV6, divalent ions can be seen to bind within a narrow region of the filter that would require at least partial dehydration of the ion.
claims.source: In the case of TRPV6, divalent ions can be seen to bind within a narrow region of the filter that would require at least partial dehydration of the ion, suggesting that ion coordination and dehydration are critical to the mechanism of divalent ion selectivity.
claims.evidence: This is an observation and inference based on structural data.

claims.claim: The S1-S4 domain and the interface of this domain with the S5-S6 pore-forming domain and the TRP box functions as a hot spot for ligands to promote opening of TRP channels.
claims.source: The wealth of available TRP channel structures underscores the extent to which the S1-S4 domain, as well as the interface of this domain with the S5-S6 pore-forming domain and the TRP box functions as a hot spot for ligands to promote opening of TRP channels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ligand-binding site analysis.

claims.claim: In cryo-EM structures of rat TRPV1 in nanodiscs, several well-defined phospholipid densities can be seen to interact simultaneously with the external membrane-exposed surface of the protein and the tarantula toxin DkTx.
claims.source: In cryo-EM structures of rat TRPV1 in nanodiscs, several well-defined phospholipid densities can be seen to interact simultaneously with the external membrane-exposed surface of the protein and the tarantula toxin DkTx (Gao et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citation.

claims.claim: A well-resolved molecule of PIP2 can be seen in flycatcher TRPM8 channels close to where Ca2+ and cooling agents bind.
claims.source: Finally, a well-resolved molecule of PIP2 can also be seen in flycatcher TRPM8 channels close to where Ca2+ and cooling agents bind, and involving basic residues in the pre-S1 helix, the S4-S5 linker, the TRP domain and the cytoplasmic MHR4 domain (Figure 8C; Yin et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on structural data and citation.

claims.claim: PIP2 is required for activation of both TRPM2 and TRPM8.
claims.source: PIP2 is required for activation of both TRPM2 and TRPM8; indeed, exogenous PIP2 analogs are sufficient to activate the TRPM8 channel at room temperature (Liu and Qin, 2005; Yudin and Rohacs, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: The analysis identifies the need for additional structures, even for the TRPV and TRPM subtypes that dominate the structural alignment.
claims.source: Although this represents an unparalleled number of related ion channel structures to work with, we were surprised that our analysis identifies the need for additional structures, even for the TRPV and TRPM subtypes that dominate our structural alignment.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comprehensive analysis performed.

claims.claim: For most TRP channels, it seems that fully open states have yet to be determined.
claims.source: In addition, for most TRP channels, it seems that fully open states have yet to be determined.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pore radius analysis.

results.result: TRP channels are a diverse family of cation-permeable ion channels with widespread biological functions and clinical significance. The family comprises seven subfamilies with 136 structures available at the time of analysis, representing a landmark achievement in cryo-EM structural biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are well-supported by extensive citations to established literature. These background claims provide context from prior work and are appropriately referenced, establishing the foundation for the current structural analysis.

results.result: TRP channels adopt a conserved tetrameric architecture with six transmembrane helices per subunit, featuring a domain-swapped arrangement where S1-S4 domains interact with adjacent S5-S6 pore domains, and most contain a TRP box helix extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 describe well-established structural features of TRP channels supported by the analyzed structures and Figure 1. These architectural features are consistently observed across the 120 structures examined and are supported by prior structural studies.

results.result: A structure-based alignment of 120 TRP channel transmembrane domains was constructed using Fr-TM-Align, addressing the challenge of low sequence identity (16%) across the family.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C19 describe the methodological approach clearly with appropriate citations. The selection of 120 structures from 136 available (resolution ≤5Å) and use of Fr-TM-Align for structure-based alignment is well-justified given the low sequence identity problem cited from prior work.

results.result: TRP channel transmembrane domains share similar global folds (TM-scores >0.6) and cluster according to subfamily assignments, with structural similarity extending to voltage-gated potassium channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by the TM-score analysis shown in Figure 2. The hierarchical clustering successfully recapitulates known subfamily relationships despite varied experimental conditions, validating the structural alignment approach. The comparison to Kv channels (TM-scores 0.46-0.78) appropriately establishes evolutionary relationships.

results.result: Pore domains are highly conserved across TRP subfamilies at the sequence level, while S1-S4 domains are more variable, with subfamily clustering more robust when based on S1-S4 domain structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and clustering comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplements 2-3). The observation that S1-S4 domains better distinguish subfamilies despite lower sequence conservation is an interesting finding supported by the data.

results.result: Xenopus laevis TRPV4 and rTRPV6 L495Q mutant structures are notable exceptions in clustering analysis, with the latter adopting a non-domain-swapped architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 identify important outliers in the structural alignment. The low TM-scores for these structures and the explanation for rTRPV6 L495Q based on its non-domain-swapped architecture (supported by citations) are well-documented. However, the reason for TRPV4's distinct clustering remains unclear, appropriately noted as requiring additional structures.

results.result: The intracellular end of S6 helices contains constrictions at four positions spanning three helical turns that likely function as a cytoplasmic gate. In 38 of 55 apo structures, pore radii ≤1.0 Å indicate non-conducting states.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by HOLE analysis (Figures 3-4) and functional studies (C28-C29 cite prior work). The identification of four constriction sites and quantification of pore radii in apo structures provides strong evidence for closed states. The inference that hydrophobic-lined narrow pores represent non-conducting states is reasonable given biophysical principles.

results.result: Wild-type human TRPV6 structures with S6 gate radii of 2.7-3.1 Å may represent open states, though this is smaller than expected given the channel's high open probability (0.25-0.9) in cellular membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 present an interesting case but with uncertainty. While TRPV6's high open probability (C33, cited) suggests structures should capture open states, the observed gate radii (2.7-3.1 Å) are at the lower limit for hydrated ion permeation. The authors appropriately express uncertainty about whether these dimensions can support the measured single-channel conductance.

results.result: Among activator-bound structures, 16 of 35 have pore radii <1.0 Å suggesting non-conducting states, while zebrafish TRPM2 bound to ADP-ribose and Ca2+ (4.4 Å radius) most likely represents an open state.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by pore radius analysis (Figures 3-4). The identification that nearly half of activator-bound structures appear closed is an important finding. The comparison of TRPM2 gate dimensions (4.4 Å) to open Kv channels (4.2-15 Å) provides strong evidence for this being an open state.

results.result: TRPV1 has high single-channel conductance (90-100 pS) and must accommodate quaternary ammonium blockers up to 10 Å diameter, suggesting the open pore exceeds 3 Å radius.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are well-supported by citations to functional studies. These constraints from electrophysiology provide important benchmarks for evaluating whether structural models represent open states, strengthening the argument that most current structures are closed.

results.result: There is no striking correlation between internal pore dimensions and the presence of activators or inhibitors, but the prevalence of cytoplasmic constrictions supports S6 functioning as a universal gate.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The lack of correlation between ligand binding and pore opening is a surprising and important negative result. The conclusion about S6 as a universal gate is appropriately conservative, acknowledging that open states remain to be determined for most channels.

results.result: The extracellular selectivity filter region is narrow across TRP subfamilies, consistent with its role in ion selectivity. TRP channels exhibit three selectivity patterns: Ca2+-selective (TRPV5/6), monovalent-selective (TRPM4/5), and non-selective.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by structural analysis (Figures 3-5) and citation to prior classification. The observation of narrow extracellular regions across subfamilies is consistent with selectivity filter function, though some structures (e.g., TRPM8) show poor resolution in this region.

results.result: Non-selective TRP channels share three conserved structural features in their selectivity filters: a conserved Gly enabling backbone bending, two backbone carbonyls positioned toward the filter base, and an acidic residue or Gln at the extracellular filter end.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 identify conserved structural features supported by analysis in Figures 4-5. The functional importance of the conserved Asp is validated by cited mutagenesis studies (C46). These features provide a structural framework for understanding non-selective permeation, though the authors appropriately note that filter dimensions vary considerably.

results.result: Ca2+-selective TRPV5 and TRPV6 channels differ from non-selective channels in three key features: Thr instead of Gly after the pore helix, an extended filter with three backbone carbonyls, and a consistently narrower pore with observed divalent ion density.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are well-supported by structural analysis (Figure 5) and functional validation through mutagenesis (C50, cited). The identification of ion density in the TRPV6 X-ray structure (C51) provides direct evidence for the proposed selectivity mechanism involving ion coordination and partial dehydration.

results.result: Monovalent-selective TRPM4 channels share features with non-selective channels but contain a conserved Gln that hydrogen bonds with adjacent backbone carbonyls, proposed to stabilize a filter permeable to hydrated monovalent but not divalent ions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 present a mechanistic hypothesis for monovalent selectivity supported by structural observations and functional validation. The mutagenesis data (C54, cited) showing that Gln mutations disrupt selectivity strongly supports the proposed mechanism. However, C53 appropriately identifies this as a hypothesis from cited work rather than proven mechanism.

results.result: Selectivity filters adopt distinct conformations in apo versus activator-bound states. In TRPV1, the filter expands from ~0.5 Å to 2.5 Å radius upon toxin binding, but functional studies show Ag+ ions can permeate in the closed state.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 document conformational changes in selectivity filters with important functional implications. The structural observation (C56) is clear, but the functional data (C57, cited) showing ion permeation in closed states challenges the hypothesis that the filter acts as a gate. This appropriately highlights the complexity of filter dynamics.

results.result: The vanilloid-binding pocket in TRPV1/TRPV2 is located at the S1-S4/S5-S6 interface and contacts 19 residues. Similar hydrophobic cavities exist in all TRP subfamilies, and vanilloids can inhibit TRPM8.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 characterize the vanilloid-binding site with structural detail (Figures 6-7) and identify its conservation across subfamilies. The observation of similar pockets in all TRP subfamilies (C61) is an important finding. C62's citation of vanilloid effects on TRPM8 supports the functional relevance of these conserved pockets.

results.result: DkTx binds to the outer pore domain perimeter of TRPV1, interacting with the extracellular S6 end and pore helix, and is selective for TRPV1 over other TRP channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 describe DkTx binding supported by structural data (Figure 7) and citations. The selectivity data (C64, cited) is important for understanding why this binding site differs from the more conserved vanilloid pocket. The large interaction surface (655-556 Å²) and lipid interactions distinguish this from small molecule binding sites.

results.result: The cooling-agent-binding pocket in TRPM8 is located entirely within the S1-S4 domain, distinct from but near the vanilloid site. Residues lining this pocket are highly conserved in TRPM2 and TRPM4.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 characterize a distinct ligand-binding site supported by structural analysis (Figures 6, 8). The conservation analysis (C67) showing high conservation in TRPM2/4 but not other subfamilies is well-documented. This raises the interesting question of why TRPM2/4 are not cooling-agent sensitive despite pocket conservation.

results.result: Ca2+ binding sites in TRPM2, TRPM4, and TRPM8 involve acidic and polar residues in S2-S3. In TRPM8, the Ca2+ site is contiguous with but does not directly contact the cooling-agent pocket.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 identify Ca2+ binding sites supported by structural data (Figure 8) and extensive citations. The spatial relationship between Ca2+ and cooling-agent sites in TRPM8 (C69) suggests potential allosteric mechanisms. The structural evidence for Ca2+ binding is strong, though the authors note these are density attributions rather than definitively identified ions.

results.result: 2-APB binds at three distinct sites in TRPV3 and one site in TRPV6. All sites show poor sequence conservation across TRP channels, despite 2-APB modulating many different TRP channels as agonist or antagonist.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 document multiple 2-APB binding sites with structural and functional validation. The lack of sequence conservation (C75) despite broad functional effects (C76, cited) is surprising and well-documented. The authors appropriately suggest that side-chain character rather than specific sequence may determine 2-APB binding, and note potential complications from 2-APB chemical instability.

results.result: CBD binds TRPV2 and ML-SA1 binds TRPML1 in a pocket at the interface between S6 and neighboring pore loop/S5/S6 helices, lined by hydrophobic residues including bulky aromatics.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 identify another conserved ligand-binding site supported by structural data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and citations to functional validation. The hydrophobic character of this pocket and its conservation suggest it may be a general lipid-binding site that can accommodate various hydrophobic ligands.

results.result: π-helix elements are frequently observed in a narrow region of S6 across TRP structures. There is a slight positive correlation between pore radius and S6 π-helix length.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 identify π-helices in S6 using DSSP analysis (Figure 10). While the observation of π-helices is supported, the correlation analysis (C80) is limited by lack of structures with large pore radii and the DSSP requirement for minimum helix length. The authors appropriately express caution about interpreting the functional role of π-helices in gating.

results.result: 310 helices are commonly found at the intracellular end of S4 helices across all TRP subfamilies, regardless of activator presence, similar to voltage-gated ion channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 document 310 helices in S4 supported by DSSP analysis (Figure 10). The observation that these occur regardless of activation state and their similarity to voltage-gated channels is interesting, though the functional significance remains unclear. The structural analysis is sound but interpretation is appropriately limited.

results.result: The analysis strongly supports that the intracellular S6 region functions as a conserved gate with constrictions at four positions. Open states remain to be determined for most TRP channels, with zebrafish TRPM2 (4.4 Å radius) most likely representing an open state.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 present major conclusions from the structural analysis. The evidence for S6 as a universal gate is strong (multiple constrictions across subfamilies). The conclusion that open states are lacking for most channels is well-supported by pore radius analysis. The identification of TRPM2 as likely open is appropriately based on comparison to Kv channels.

results.result: Structures of TRPV6 and TRPM4 have led to working hypotheses for divalent and monovalent selectivity mechanisms, with TRPV6 showing ion binding in a narrow filter region requiring partial dehydration.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 summarize mechanistic hypotheses appropriately identified as working models. The observation of ion density in TRPV6 (C87) provides direct structural evidence for the dehydration mechanism. The authors appropriately note these are hypotheses requiring further validation through higher-resolution structures and MD simulations.

results.result: The S1-S4 domain and its interface with the S5-S6 pore domain and TRP box functions as a hot spot for ligand binding that promotes channel opening.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 synthesizes the ligand-binding site analysis into a unifying conclusion. The identification of this region as a ligand hot spot is well-supported by the multiple binding sites documented (vanilloids, cooling agents, Ca2+, 2-APB, etc.). This represents an important structural principle for understanding TRP channel pharmacology.

results.result: Well-defined phospholipid densities interact with TRPV1 and DkTx in nanodisc structures. PIP2 binds TRPM8 near Ca2+ and cooling-agent sites and is required for TRPM2 and TRPM8 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 document lipid interactions supported by structural observations and functional studies (C91, cited). The PIP2 binding site in TRPM8 (C90) is particularly well-resolved and involves multiple domains. These observations highlight the importance of lipid regulation, though the authors appropriately note that most lipid densities are insufficiently resolved for definitive identification.

results.result: Despite analyzing 120 structures, the study identifies the need for additional structures, particularly fully open states for most TRP channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 present important conclusions about gaps in structural coverage. The identification that open states are lacking despite extensive structural work is a key finding supported by the pore radius analysis. This appropriately frames future research directions and acknowledges limitations of current structural data.
